questionsToConsider: Which scanners in your range do you actually want to recommend, and what separates them for a buyer?
Do you want inspection and large-site enquiries to reach a person before any product page?
Should the budget ranges show real prices from your catalogue, or stay as tiers?
Is a demo or a sample scan something you can offer at the end of each result?
guide.howToUseResponses: Read the surfaces and environment answers before anyone calls a lead: a buyer scanning black, shiny parts on site needs a different demo from one scanning resin prints on a desk. Sort by the use answer to see which result your quiz sends most people to, and check that you stock enough of it. Export to CSV to hand inspection and site-scanning leads to your technical team.
customizeSteps: Rename each result after the real model or product family you sell, and adjust the budget ranges to match your prices.
Change the options in the final question if your range splits differently, keeping one branch per result.
Embed the quiz on your scanner category page or share the link in replies to enquiries.

faqs.q: What should a 3D scanner buyer ask before choosing one?
faqs.a: What they will scan, how big it is, how fine the detail must be, and what surfaces are involved. Where they scan and what they do with the data afterwards matters just as much as resolution.

faqs.q: Why ask about shiny, dark or clear surfaces?
faqs.a: Those surfaces reflect or absorb the light most scanners rely on, so they often need a different scanner type or a scanning spray. Knowing about them early avoids a disappointing first scan.

faqs.q: How does this quiz decide which scanner to recommend?
faqs.a: The final question about what the scans are for routes each person to one of four results. You can change the options and point each one at any result you write.

faqs.q: Can I use this quiz to collect sales leads?
faqs.a: Yes. The email question is optional, and every answer is saved to your dashboard so your team can follow up with the context already in hand.

endings.title: An entry-level desktop or handheld scanner 🖨️
endings.bodyMd: For printing and personal projects, a desktop turntable scanner for small objects, or an entry-level handheld for anything bigger, is the easiest place to start. They give you print-ready models without a steep learning curve. If you scan shiny or dark objects, a light coat of scanning spray makes a big difference.

endings.title: A professional handheld scanner 🛠️
endings.bodyMd: For reverse engineering you need clean, accurate meshes that drop straight into CAD. A handheld laser or blue-light scanner copes with shiny and dark parts better than entry-level models, and it goes to the part instead of the part coming to the desk. We'll follow up with the models that fit the sizes you scan.

endings.title: A metrology-grade scanner 📐
endings.bodyMd: Inspection work needs measured, repeatable accuracy with a calibration certificate behind it, not just a nice-looking model. A metrology-grade blue-light or laser scanner, paired with inspection software, lets you compare every part to its CAD file. Our team will get in touch to talk through tolerances before you buy.

endings.title: A long-range scanner 🏛️
endings.bodyMd: Rooms, buildings and sites are a different job from objects on a bench. A long-range laser scanner captures whole spaces from a few set-ups and stitches them together, and works outdoors where handheld scanners struggle. We'll send the options that suit the size of the spaces you record.
